sections.text: Methods are functions that belong to a type. You write them inside an impl block. The first parameter, self, is the value the method is called on.
&self borrows the value to read it. &mut self borrows it to change it. Plain self takes ownership.

Every function in an impl block is an associated function: it belongs to the type. The ones that take self are methods, called with a dot. The ones without self are called with :: and are often used as constructors named new:
You've already used associated functions: String::from is one.
Inside an impl you can write Self instead of the type name, e.g. fn new() -> Self. Method calls auto-reference, so r.area() works whether r is a value or a reference.

exercise.prompt: Add a method perimeter(&self) -> u32 to Rectangle that returns 2 * (width + height). Then change the println! so it prints both, using r.area() and r.perimeter(). It should print: area 12, perimeter 14
